requirements.title: Statement keywords do not reserve same-spelled names
requirements.definition: A name with the same spelling as a statement keyword is allowed in a context where the grammar expects a name. This admission does not alter token spelling, case equivalence, implicit typing, declaration ordering or the statement syntax that uses the keyword literally.

pending.same-spelling-name-admission: PENDING compile and run a program with IMPLICIT NONE and variables named if, read, unit, kind and integer initialized to distinct integer sentinels; assign and check exact values in contexts parsed as names.
pending.statement-keyword-token-separation: PENDING companion source uses a conditional construct and READ/WRITE statements plus same-spelled variables in separate declarations, checking variable values survive; mutate the variable spellings to ordinary names to prove the oracle is not keyword-text specific.

requirements.oracle: The plan observes exact integer values of same-spelled names after declaration, assignment and use. Statement execution itself is checked only through owners of the corresponding statement syntax.
requirements.oracle_limitation: This is not a claim that keywords can appear in arbitrary name positions, that malformed tokens are accepted, or that IMPLICIT NONE changes keyword status. Parser recovery text and case-specific diagnostics are not asserted.
requirements.dependencies: 6.2.2 owns name spelling and length; 6.3.2 owns token separation; 8.7 owns IMPLICIT NONE; individual statement forms own their literal keyword syntax and execution effects.

accounting.rationale: PDF65 combines the definition of statement keywords, the non-reservation admission for same-spelled names and examples; the fine units split those roles.
Statement keywords appear literally in syntax rules and the unmodified term keyword in descriptive text denotes this meaning. Tokenization and source form remain with Clause 6.
The listed spellings IF, READ, UNIT, KIND and INTEGER illustrate statement keywords and specifier/type contexts; the examples do not create new syntax beyond their owning statement rules.
